title: Excelsior's rehearsed hymns and bands in the Claiborne neutral ground
summary: Excelsior's hymns and marches were pre-rehearsed. Ernie describes the Claiborne neutral ground, where bands played on Sundays, and the lakefront bands.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: I was going to ask one thing about the Excelsior band. Did they ever play hymns without using their music? Say if they'd play like By and By or Glory Land, did they ever play things like that?

Yeah, they played those numbers, they played those numbers, but this was the irony. Not that they played it without music, but they had already rehearsed that music that they needed. They played the same way every time. See, right now, if, right now we go out and they call us and they call a number. We haven't rehearsed it, we just know the number. They just knock it off. As soon as the trumpet player, you know, we know with keys and we start playing, see. But they had done rehearsed that, they wouldn't even need it. I mean, they didn't rehearse the music, they'd leave that horn. They just bring the funeral marches or maybe some other little marches that they want to play. And when they get ready to play by and by or walk through the streets of the city or one of those other hymns or Panama Rag or something, that music has been rehearsed. They rehearse two or three times a week. It's like a big band, they did. See, they had those halls, see. And those big bands sometimes would be hired out more often than we were because, see, right there on Aldean and Claiborne. All these are Claiborne there, in that neutral ground. There was a circle there with concrete about three feet high with an iron rail in there. Remember that? That hasn't been long, tip and taken up. Aldean's right in the circle. It came up a few years ago. You see where the Trammet market is now, where Jerusalem is breaking, that market used to be in the neutral ground. That used to run just about a half a block from Claiborne all the way to Moray Street. And the very market streetcar used to pass through it, see. And when you leave out there, they had a big tower near the end of Claiborne Street where they used to ring the bell at 9 o'clock for the children to get inside. See, I remember that good. And right just on this side of Claiborne in the neutral ground, man, there was a big ring and a big iron rail fence there. And where the shed, where they tore the shed down. And every Sunday one of those big bands would be playing in there.
Somebody hire him for the job?

Yeah, it's like a city would hire him, see? And sometimes they'd have a white band up at St. Mary's Playground, up on Magazine Street and that's it, but every Sunday, and out on the lakefront they'd have them big bands like that. And it'd take like Buddy Petit and Chris Crom, they'd be playing at them out on the lakefront, West End, Spanish folk, Captain Madison, those places and like that. Well, I played several of those songs before they broke those camps down. I had a chance to play plenty of those.
I think, Harold, you mentioned once about, you mentioned once there was a bell on some of them. No, Clever, on Orleans, at the same time.
It was a little better than 50 feet high and they took the whole neutral ground on the floor. It was a tile. We used to pry them off. They used to pull these makers, we used to pry them off.
Oh, yeah, the police was coming.
